Runs of emoji: the sequences writers build

Source: R/emoji-access.R
emoji_runs.Rd

emoji_runs() returns one row per run of emoji: a maximal stretch of emoji with nothing but white space between them, or nothing at all with sep = "adjacent". Runs are the unit the literature on emoji sequences annotates. Reduplication, one emoji repeated for emphasis, is the dominant multi-emoji pattern (Cohn, Engelen and Schilperoord 2019), and repetitive sequences are one of the few emoji features that tell people's text from a language model's.

Usage

emoji_runs(
  data,
  text,
  sep = c("whitespace", "adjacent"),
  presentation = "emoji"
)

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble containing a text column. Grouped data frames are accepted. The verbs that work a row at a time (adding columns, or keeping and expanding rows) carry the grouping through to their result, as dplyr::mutate() and dplyr::filter() do. The verbs that pool across rows – the counts, the co-occurrence edge lists, the time series – warn that they ignore the grouping and return one corpus-wide answer.

text

The text column to scan, supplied unquoted. Any atomic column is accepted and read as character, so a factor works and a numeric, Date or logical one simply contains no emoji. A list column – or a data-frame column – is refused rather than coerced, because coercing one deparses it and the emoji found would be in the code rather than in your data. What counts as an emoji is the same in every verb; see the Detection section of tidyEmoji for the one case that surprises people, code points that are emoji only when they carry U+FE0F.

sep

What may stand between two emoji of one run: "whitespace" (the default) or "adjacent" (nothing).

presentation

Which code points count as emoji: "emoji" (the default) or "any".

  • "emoji" requires emoji presentation, so U+2764 U+FE0F is an emoji and the bare U+2764 is not. This is the default and it will stay the default: widening it would silently recount every corpus already analysed.

  • "any" also reads the text-presentation spellings Unicode lists for an emoji (the bare heart, U+263A, U+2714, a keycap without its selector), because several keyboards emit them. It never reads the copyright, registered and trade-mark signs (U+00A9, U+00AE, U+2122), which are typography far more often than they are emoji.

"any" only ever adds occurrences: everything "emoji" finds, it finds too, in the same place. emoji_coverage() reports how many it adds and how many of those a lexicon can score, which is the cost of the choice in one number. Every verb that counts, scores or rewrites the emoji in a text column takes this argument, so counts still agree across the package for whichever value you use. The flag verbs do not need it, since a flag has no text-presentation form.

Value

A tibble with one row per run, carrying the columns of data (rows without emoji contribute none), and .row_number, .emoji_run (the number of the run within its row), .emoji_run_start and .emoji_run_end (code-point offsets), .emoji_run_length (emoji in it), .emoji_run_n_distinct, .emoji_run_glyphs (its emoji, written together), .emoji_run_is_reduplication (more than one emoji, all the same) and .emoji_run_position ("begin", "mid", "end" or "only"). A grouped input stays grouped.

Details

What separates two runs. With sep = "whitespace", the default and what the annotators of the sequence literature did, white space may sit inside a run, so "x x x" spaced out is one run; with "adjacent" only emoji written directly together are. White space is Unicode's White_Space, as everywhere in the package. The choice matters: the bundled sample holds 1,038 runs under the default and 1,148 under "adjacent", and how far apart the two are depends on how the text was written. Under the default 37.5% of its 1,454 emoji sit in a run of two or more, and 19 of its 129 such runs are reduplications. A zero-width-joiner sequence that counts as its parts (see the Detection section of tidyEmoji) is one run of those parts.

Position. A run is at the "begin" of its text when only white space and punctuation come before it, at the "end" when only they come after it, "only" when both are true, and "mid" otherwise.

Runs are not n-grams: emoji_ngrams() slides a window of fixed length over the emoji of a text, where a run is a maximal span of any length.

References

Cohn, N., Engelen, J. and Schilperoord, J. (2019). The grammar of emoji? Constraints on communicative pictorial sequencing. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications 4, 33. doi:10.1186/s41235-019-0177-0

See also

emoji_features() for one row per emoji, with its run; emoji_a11y_check(); emoji_ngrams().

Examples

d <- data.frame(text = c("wow \U0001f600\U0001f600\U0001f600",
                         "\U0001f600 ok \U0001f389",
                         "\U0001f600\U0001f389"))
emoji_runs(d, text)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 10
#>   text  .row_number .emoji_run .emoji_run_start .emoji_run_end .emoji_run_length
#>   <chr>       <int>      <int>            <int>          <int>             <int>
#> 1 wow …           1          1                5              7                 3
#> 2 😀 ok…           2          1                1              1                 1
#> 3 😀 ok…           2          2                6              6                 1
#> 4 😀🎉            3          1                1              2                 2
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: .emoji_run_n_distinct <int>, .emoji_run_glyphs <chr>,
#> #   .emoji_run_is_reduplication <lgl>, .emoji_run_position <chr>
